evidence_quotes.quote: Part 1 of this chapter describes the law and policy framework for the right to water in South Africa, where the constitutional right has been concretised in a number of legislative and policy documents including the Water Services Act (WSA), the National Water Act (NWA) and the Free Basic Water Policy.
Parts 2, 3 and 4 turn to some of the challenges observed in the realisation of the right to water which relate more specifically to the application of economic policies to water.

In order to ensure the financial sustainability of the provision of free water, municipalities are required to adopt a block tariff system according to which the cost of water increases with usage, subject to the requirement that the first block of water for up to six kilolitres per household per month should be provided free.

The other side of the coin is that accessibility of water services is contingent upon ability to pay. This has led in South Africa to rising use of water service disconnections, the installation of pre-paid water meters, and a certain level of privatisation of the water services sector.
The WSA sets forth legal procedural and substantive criteria applicable to limitations and disconnections of water services by water providers. Overall, such procedures must be fair and equitable.

criterion_notes.c1: The chapter examines household and community access to drinking water and basic sanitation services in post-apartheid South Africa, including physical accessibility, basic water quantity (25 litres per person per day / 6 kilolitres per household per month), affordability, and service disconnections.
criterion_notes.c2: Both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading are satisfied: under the plain wording, the chapter examines constitutional, statutory, regulatory, and governance frameworks (1996 Constitution Section 27, National Water Act 1998, Water Services Act 1997, and Free Basic Water Policy 2001); under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it specifically analyses rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access, including block tariff and cost-recovery rules, the 6-kilolitre free basic water entitlement, statutory procedural safeguards for service limitations and disconnections (WSA Section 4(3)), enforcement via pre-paid water meters, and utility corporatisation/privatisation structures.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3: this book chapter is a doctrinal legal and human-rights policy analysis and narrative commentary. It contains no primary empirical data collection, no qualitative or quantitative empirical methodology, and no systematic empirical synthesis, relying solely on constitutional/statutory texts, UN human-rights documents, court filings/decisions, and secondary literature. Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence).
criterion_notes.c4: Although the chapter narratively discusses access disparities, affordability barriers, municipal arrears, and service disconnections citing secondary policy documents and litigation affidavits, it conducts no empirical measurement or systematic synthesis of access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the chapter is a non-empirical doctrinal and policy overview, there is no empirical study design, sample, or analytical unit of observation from which an empirical population-exposure-outcome relationship can be extracted.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, which is eligible without translation.

study_design: Doctrinal legal and policy commentary / narrative overview (non-empirical)
exposure: South Africa's water law and policy framework, including Constitution Section 27, the Water Services Act (1997), the Free Basic Water Policy (6 kilolitres/household/month block tariff rule), cost-recovery pricing, utility corporatisation/privatisation, disconnection rules, and pre-paid water meters
outcome: Narrative discussion of household drinking water access, affordability, municipal arrears, and service disconnections (no empirical outcome measured)
rationale: This 2010 book chapter by Gowlland-Gualtieri examines South Africa's post-apartheid legal and policy framework for household water access (satisfying c1 and both the plain and narrow rule-type readings of c2, covering Free Basic Water block tariffs, cost-recovery rules, WSA disconnection safeguards, pre-paid water meters, and privatisation/corporatisation). However, the work is purely a doctrinal legal and human-rights policy overview synthesizing constitutional and statutory texts, UN documents, court pleadings, and secondary sources, with no primary data, no empirical methods, and no systematic empirical synthesis. Per Exclusion Criteria 1 and 6, it is excluded under code E05 (No empirical evidence).
